raw:
These hypotheses come from my prior knowledge of NAS-Bench-201 behavior; I haven't run any of the experiments.

The main patterns I'm relying on:
- Adding a conv to an edge helps less when the cell already has a strong path to the output through other edges, because of diminishing returns.
- Removing or weakening an edge hurts more when it is the only strong path.
- Edges into node 3 are largely interchangeable, so the edit's effect depends on what the other edges into node 3 hold.

Each hypothesis below pairs an edit with a condition on one parent edge.

1. Edge 3 -> nor_conv_3x3 gains more when edge 3 currently holds none than when it holds something else. Replacing none with a conv adds a new direct path, while replacing skip or pool is a smaller upgrade.
2. Edge 5 -> none costs more when edge 4 is none than when it is not, because edge 5 then becomes a key path into node 3.
3. Edge 0 -> none costs more when edge 1 is none than when it is not, because the 0->1 path is then needed for any route through node 1.
4. Edge 0 -> nor_conv_3x3 gains more when edge 0 currently holds none than when it does not, since it replaces a missing connection.
5. Edge 2 -> skip_connect costs more when edge 2 currently holds nor_conv_3x3 than when it does not, since it replaces a conv.
6. Edge 1 -> skip_connect costs more when edge 1 currently holds nor_conv_3x3 than when it does not.
7. Edge 4 -> avg_pool_3x3 costs more when edge 4 currently holds nor_conv_3x3 than when it does not.
8. Edge 5 -> nor_conv_3x3 gains more when edge 5 currently holds none than when it does not.
9. Edge 3 -> skip_connect gains more when edge 3 currently holds none than when it does not, because it adds a residual path where conv or pool replacement would lose capacity.
10. Edge 1 -> nor_conv_1x1 gains more when edge 1 currently holds none than when it does not.
